message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing images, now also for highly parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few (2–32) high‑performance cores. | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores. |
| **Execution model** | Serial or lightly parallel; each core can handle complex branching and large caches. | Massive data‑parallelism; many cores execute the same instruction on different data (SIMD). |
| **Clock speed** | Higher clock speeds (≈2–4 GHz) because each core does more work per cycle. | Lower clock speeds (≈0.5–1 GHz) because each core is simpler. |
| **Cache hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core to reduce memory latency. | Small per‑core caches; relies on high memory bandwidth instead. |
| **Memory access** | Random access patterns are efficient; can fetch arbitrary data quickly. | Optimized for contiguous, coalesced memory accesses; random access is costly. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex, with many control‑flow instructions (branches, jumps). | Simple, mostly arithmetic/logic; limited branching. |
| **Typical workloads** | Single‑threaded or lightly threaded tasks, OS kernel, database queries, web servers. | Tasks that can be split into many independent operations: image/video processing, scientific simulations, machine‑learning inference/training, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Energy efficiency** | More power per core due to higher performance. | Very power‑efficient for parallel workloads because many cores share a single power domain. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional CPU programming (C/C++, Java, etc.) with multi‑threading libraries. | Requires parallel programming frameworks (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan, DirectX Raytracing, Metal). |

### Why the difference matters

- **Serial vs. Parallel**: CPUs excel at tasks that require complex decision making and low latency. GPUs shine when you can process many data items in the same way simultaneously.
- **Latency vs. Bandwidth**: CPUs have low memory latency thanks to large caches. GPUs have high memory bandwidth but higher latency, so they’re best when you can keep all cores busy with large data streams.
- **Flexibility vs. Specialization**: CPUs are general‑purpose; GPUs are specialized for throughput‑heavy, data‑parallel workloads.

In practice, modern systems use both: the CPU handles the “control” side of applications, while the GPU accelerates the “data” side. This hybrid approach is especially common in gaming, AI, scientific computing, and real‑time analytics.
